channel.title: Phys.org - latest science and technology news stories
channel.description: Phys.org internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: New research shows how water would behave on the moon
item.description: As humanity looks toward future bases on the moon, plant cultivation will be critical for sustaining life there. Plants can provide food, oxygen, medicine, water purification and waste recycling, making them indispensable for lunar development.

item.title: Multilingual readers report higher enjoyment and more daily reading, survey finds
item.description: The U.K.'s National Year of Reading is asking people across the country to "go all in" on reading. But this invitation raises questions for many families: reading what, in which language and in what form?

item.title: How much are the world's oceans warming? New method reveals double-digit percentage gaps from climate models
item.description: The world's oceans behave like a thermometer: As the water warms, it expands and sea levels rise. Geodesy researchers at the University of Bonn are able to measure this and determine how much the oceans are warming. For individual ocean basins, their method has revealed significant deviations from model calculations—in some cases in the double-digit percentage range.

item.title: New study reveals how national cyber positions can shape the future of international law
item.description: Nations should do more to reduce uncertainty about the legal value of their positions on cyber activities, a new study says.

item.title: A 'reality check' for lab-grown human embryo models
item.description: University of Sydney researchers have developed a new way to test how closely lab-grown biological models resemble real human embryos, finding that while some models perform well, none yet fully capture the complexity of early human development.

item.title: Multitasking in magenta: Colored solar panels could help farms grow crops and generate electricity on shared land
item.description: Broccoli grown under magenta solar panels absorbed sunlight more efficiently than plants grown out in the open, according to a study to be published Oct. 2 in Cell Reports Physical Science.

item.title: First U.S. tomato spotted wilt virus clone could speed development of disease-resistant crops
item.description: New technology from Texas A&M AgriLife Research could be a major step toward bringing disease-resistant peppers and tomatoes to growers' fields and lowering costs at grocery stores.

item.title: Natural-material bricks aim to give urban birds alternatives to nesting with trash
item.description: It's spring, and Australian birds are building their nests. But with what? Alongside grass and twigs, birds are collecting our trash. In 2023, a global study found litter in the nests of 176 different bird species, with common culprits including cigarette butts, plastic bags and fishing nets.

item.title: Uranium forms rare triple bond with carbon in newly isolated compound
item.description: In a study published in Nature Chemistry, an international team of researchers from Germany and the U.K., including chemists from The University of Manchester, has synthesized and characterized what they describe as the first isolable uranium Fischer-type carbyne, a compound in which carbon forms an unusual triple-bond interaction with uranium.

item.title: Survey finds burnout is top challenge for independent local news publishers
item.description: More than 55% of publishers of independent local news organizations cite burnout as a concern, and about 52% view balancing journalism with business operations as one of their most pressing challenges, a new survey finds.

item.title: Protons ride moving waves to reach record energy with long-pulse lasers
item.description: Imagine a proton catching a wave and surfing it to gain speed. While the imagery may seem wild, the premise of laser-driven ion acceleration has promise as an alternative to conventional accelerators. However, the ultrathin targets used to drive this increase in ion energy are vulnerable to the weak prepulse that precedes the main high-intensity laser pulse, meaning an adaptation in the process is necessary.

item.title: Are Australia's native bees thriving or declining?
item.description: It's a sight to behold.

item.title: A conservation success story for New Zealand's heaviest insect
item.description: The success of a large-scale recovery program for wētāpunga/Little Barrier giant wētā, New Zealand's heaviest insect, has been officially documented in the New Zealand Journal of Zoology.

item.title: Birdsong tells only part of a forest's story: Evolutionary trees reveal the rest
item.description: Birds calling back and forth in the morning make up one of the defining sounds of tropical forests. We're likely to assume that hearing or seeing more types of birds indicates a healthy forest.

item.title: Two active magma reservoirs may lie beneath Masaya volcano, near 2 million people
item.description: Masaya volcano in Nicaragua sits within 13 miles (21 kilometers) of 2 million people and is a popular tourist destination due to its lava lake. Penn State researchers recently found evidence of two new magma sources under the active volcano, highlighting what they called the critical importance of understanding transitions in volcanic behavior and shallow magma processes, especially when they potentially pose hazards to local communities.

item.title: Rethinking smart cities: An open-source tool for urban data collection
item.description: A large part of urban planning involves navigating how people experience a place. That kind of insight can require collecting data at a level of detail that large-scale datasets cannot provide.

item.title: A laser that stays locked without active control
item.description: EPFL researchers have developed a chip-based laser that keeps a very stable frequency across its tested operating range, without needing active electronic control. Their research is published in the journal Nature Photonics.

item.title: The vanishing of aurochs: Genetic evidence reveals multiple stressors at the same time
item.description: Aurochs, the ancient ancestors of modern cattle, once roamed large parts of Europe, Asia and northern Africa. New research by an international team led by Lund University indicates that multiple factors contributed to their demise in northern Europe—one of the first areas where they became extinct.

item.title: Will AI make corporate communication sound the same?
item.description: Companies that use AI tools to write their earnings presentations are sounding increasingly alike, a new study finds.

item.title: Nepal disaster highlights risks for NZ mountains
item.description: Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) School of Earth and Environment senior lecturer Dr. Robinson was part of an international research team investigating the Aug. 26 disaster, when a massive rock and ice avalanche in the Himalaya rapidly transformed into a devastating debris flood.

item.title: Astronomers discover the lowest-mass double neutron star system to date
item.description: Neutron stars, the extremely dense remains of massive stars that exploded at the end of their lives, are widely studied astrophysical objects. Some of these stars, known as pulsars, spin and send out beams of radio waves, making them appear to pulse as the beams sweep past Earth.

item.title: How deep do AI relationships really go? Attachment theory expert explains
item.description: Attachment is the term psychologists use for the most significant relationships that hold people's lives together. But what makes an attachment relationship different from all others? According to the pioneering American–Canadian developmental psychologist Mary Ainsworth, it must meet the following six conditions.

item.title: Bushfire simulation reveals green strategy that could cut Australia's fire threat
item.description: New modeling shows irrigating low-flammability vegetation substantially reduces the predicted spread and intensity of wildfires, which could give communities critical extra preparation time, according to a University of the Sunshine Coast study.

item.title: Study links hurricane exposure to higher eviction risk for renters
item.description: Hurricanes can displace renters even when their homes suffer no damage, according to new research led by Rowan University urban planner Qian He.

item.title: The economy is resilient: Why do many Americans feel differently? An expert explains
item.description: Even as the Federal Reserve moves to raise interest rates for the first time in three years, many of the metrics that economists rely on to gauge the overall health of the economy—like jobs reports, the unemployment rate and the stock market—have looked relatively strong in recent months. Despite this, only about 24% of Americans rated the economy as "good" or "excellent" in a recent Pew Research Center survey.

item.title: Q&A: How can marketers use AI effectively—without losing human judgment?
item.description: As marketers increasingly turn to artificial intelligence (AI) tools to create content and improve the efficiency of their workflows, a new study by a Penn State researcher and collaborators proposes an approach to deploying AI-generated marketing content at scale while reducing the need for costly and time-consuming traditional testing.

item.title: Europe's hottest summer caused record heat stress: Monitor
item.description: A record 52% of Europe was exposed to intense heat stress during the exceptionally hot summer that seared the continent this year, the EU's climate monitor said Friday.

item.title: Return of swarming moth spectacle has Australia in a flutter
item.description: Moth swarms so thick they can blot out the stars are fluttering across Australia, heralding a migratory spectacle unseen since the creature's brush with extinction nearly 10 years ago.

item.title: Astronauts arrive at International Space Station on the quickest US express flight yet
item.description: Four astronauts pulled up at the International Space Station on Thursday after launching on an eight-hour express that set a U.S. speed record.

item.title: Underwater umbrellas for coral reefs could help protect against heat damage
item.description: High sea temperatures driven by the climate crisis damage corals, bleaching them ghostly white and killing them. While restoration of dead reefs is possible, it's difficult and expensive, and restored corals are vulnerable to future heat waves. Finding ways to stop or slow the damage to existing reefs is crucial.
